title: حِكَايَةُ الْقُنْفُذِ وَالْوَرَشَانِ
part: Night 152 · The Fox and the Crow ends / The Hedgehog and the Ringdove / The Thief and His Ape / The Sparrow and the Peacock
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 753–760 (Night 152, continuing directly from nights-151), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 152 ends the tale of the fox and the crow and moves through a chain of short fables on cunning and on aping one's betters. The crow finishes his fable of the falcon who, grown old, lives by guile instead of strength, and tells of the sparrow who tried to carry off a ram as an eagle carries off a lamb and was caught in its wool; the fox slinks home. Shahrazād then tells of the hedgehog who played the hermit to talk a pair of ringdoves out of their dates and then into his den — and the ringdove's warning tale of two sharpers who poisoned each other; of a thief who sold a bundle of rags unseen, and the wife who warned her husband with the tale of the weaver who copied an acrobat's leap and broke his neck — advice the husband ignored, to his ruin; and of the sparrow, vizier to the peacock, king of the birds, who for all his caution is taken in the fowler's net, ending in two lines of verse on fate. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ وَالْخَمْسُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāniyatu wa-al-khamsūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the second-and-fifty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and fifty-second night,
sentences.n: al-thāniya, “the second”, is the ordinal, feminine to agree with layla; al-khamsūn, “fifty”, keeps its cardinal form and is joined by wa-.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْغُرَابَ قَالَ زَعَمُوا أَنَّ صَقْرًا كَانَ جَبَّارًا عَنِيدًا فِي أَيَّامِ شَبِيبَتِهِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-ghurāba qāla zaʿamū anna ṣaqran kāna jabbāran ʿanīdan fī ayyāmi shabībatihi
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the crow said: They-claimed that a falcon was tyrannical, stubborn, in the days of his youth;
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the crow said, “They say that there was once a falcon, a tyrant and headstrong in the days of his youth.
sentences.n: The night takes up the fable where the last one broke off, repeating its first words. shabība, “youth, the prime of life”. The shadda in جبّارا is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ تَفْزَعُ مِنْهُ سِبَاعُ الطَّيْرِ وَسِبَاعُ الْبَرِّ وَلَايَسْلَمُ مِنْ شَرِّةِ أَحَدٌ
sentences.tr: wa-kānat tafzaʿu minhu sibāʿu al-ṭayri wa-sibāʿu al-barri wa-lā yaslamu min sharrihi aḥadun
sentences.l: And there-used-to fear from-him the beasts-of-prey of the birds and the beasts-of-prey of the land, and not-was-safe from his-evil anyone.
sentences.i: The birds of prey and the beasts of prey of the land alike went in fear of him, and no one was safe from his malice.
sentences.n: sibāʿ, plural of sabuʿ, “beast of prey”: sibāʿ al-ṭayr are the predatory birds, sibāʿ al-barr the predators of the land. The print runs ولا يسلم together as one word, and writes the pronoun of sharrihi, “his evil”, with a tāʾ marbūṭa (شرة for شرّه), a habit of this edition.

sentences.t: وَلَهُ وَقَائِعُ كَثِيرَةٌ فِي ظُلْمِهِ وَتَجَبُّرِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-lahu waqāʾiʿu kathīratun fī ẓulmihi wa-tajabburihi
sentences.l: And to-him (were) deeds many in his-oppression and his-tyrannising.
sentences.i: Many were the deeds told of his oppression and his tyranny.
sentences.n: waqāʾiʿ, plural of wāqiʿa, “event, encounter”, here the deeds he had done. The shadda in تجبّره is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ دَأْبُ هَذَا الصَّقْرِ الْأَذَى لِسَائِرِ الطُّيُورِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna daʾbu hādhā al-ṣaqri al-adhā li-sāʾiri al-ṭuyūri
sentences.l: And was the habit of this falcon the harm to all the birds.
sentences.i: It was this falcon's habit to do harm to every other bird.
sentences.n: daʾb, “habit, wont”, is the subject of kāna; al-adhā, “harm”, its predicate, accusative but showing no ending on its final alif.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا مَرَّتْ عَلَيْهِ السِّنُونَ ضَعُفَتْ قُوَّتُهُ وَانْهَدَّ حَيْلُهُ وَجَاعَ وَاشْتَدَّ جَهْدُهُ بَعْدَ فَقْدِ قُوَّتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā marrat ʿalayhi al-sinūna ḍaʿufat quwwatuhu wa-inhadda ḥayluhu wa-jāʿa wa-ishtadda jahduhu baʿda faqdi quwwatihi
sentences.l: And when passed over-him the years, weakened his-strength and collapsed his-might, and he-hungered, and grew-hard his-distress after the loss of his-strength.
sentences.i: But when the years had passed over him, his strength failed and his might crumbled; he went hungry, and his hardship grew heavy once his strength was gone.
sentences.n: inhadda, “to be demolished, collapse”, said of a wall; ḥayl, “might, power”. jahd, “hardship, distress”. The shadda in مرّت is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَأَجْمَعَ رَأْيَهُ عَلَى أَنْ يَأْتِيَ مَجْمَعَ الطَّيْرِ فَيَأْكُلَ مَا يَفْضُلُ مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ajmaʿa raʾyahu ʿalā an yaʾtiya majmaʿa al-ṭayri fa-yaʾkula mā yafḍulu minhā
sentences.l: So he-gathered his-opinion upon that he-come-to the gathering-place of the birds and eat what is-left-over from-them.
sentences.i: So he made up his mind to go to the place where the birds gathered and eat whatever they left over.
sentences.n: ajmaʿa raʾyahu ʿalā, “to resolve upon”, literally “to gather one's judgement on”. fa-yaʾkula is subjunctive, joined to an yaʾtiya. minhā, “from them”, is feminine because al-ṭayr, a collective, is treated as a feminine plural.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ صَارَ قُوَّتُهُ بِالْحِيلَةِ بَعْدَ الْقُوَّةِ وَالشِّدَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika ṣāra quwwatuhu bi-al-ḥīlati baʿda al-quwwati wa-al-shiddati
sentences.l: And at that, became his-strength by-the ruse after the strength and the force.
sentences.i: And so, where once he had lived by strength and force, now he lived by guile.
sentences.n: The print points the word قُوّته, quwwatuhu, “his strength”: “his strength came to lie in guile after it had lain in force”. The masculine verb ṣāra with the feminine quwwa is loose agreement. The two words look alike unpointed, and both run through this fable: quwwa, “strength”, and qūt, “food, sustenance”, which the print points in the next sentence but one (قُوتك). Read with qūt, the sentence would say “his food came by guile”. The shadda and damma are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَأَنْتَ كَذَلِكَ أَيُّهَا الثَّعْلَبُ إِنْ عَدِمْتَ قُوَّتَكَ مَا عَدِمْتَ خِدَاعَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-anta ka-dhālika ayyuhā al-thaʿlabu in ʿadimta quwwataka mā ʿadimta khidāʿaka
sentences.l: And you (are) like-that, O you the fox: if you-have-lost your-strength, not have-you-lost your-deceit.
sentences.i: And you are the same, fox: you may have lost your strength, but you have not lost your cunning.
sentences.n: ʿadima, “to lose, be bereft of”. The two halves are built in parallel, ʿadimta quwwataka / mā ʿadimta khidāʿaka.

sentences.t: وَلَسْتُ أَشُكُّ فِي أَنَّ مَا تَطْلُبُهُ مِنْ صُحْبَتِي حِيلَةٌ عَلَى قُوتِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-lastu ashukku fī anna mā taṭlubuhu min ṣuḥbatī ḥīlatun ʿalā qūtika
sentences.l: And I-am-not doubting in that what you-seek of my-companionship (is) a ruse for your-food.
sentences.i: I do not doubt that this friendship you are asking of me is a trick to get yourself a meal.
sentences.n: shakka fī, “to doubt (something)”: the verb chooses fī. ḥīla ʿalā, “a ruse to obtain”. The print points قُوتك, qūt, “food”: the falcon's fable was about food, and so is the fox's friendship. The damma on ولستُ and the shadda and damma on اشكُّ are also the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَا كُنْتُ مِمَّنْ يَطْرَحُ وَيَضَعُ يَدَهُ فِي يَدِكَ لِأَنَّ اللَّهَ أَعْطَانِي قُوَّةً فِي جَنَاحِي وَحَذَرًا فِي نَفْسِي وَبَصَرًا فِي عَيْنِي
sentences.tr: fa-lā kuntu mimman yaṭraḥu wa-yaḍaʿu yadahu fī yadika li-anna Allāha aʿṭānī quwwatan fī janāḥī wa-ḥadharan fī nafsī wa-baṣaran fī ʿaynī
sentences.l: So may-I-not be among-those-who throw and put his-hand in your-hand, because God has-given-me strength in my-wing, and wariness in my-soul, and sight in my-eye.
sentences.i: Never may I be one of those who throw themselves down and put their hand in yours! For God has given me strength in my wing, wariness in my heart and keen sight in my eye.
sentences.n: fa-lā kuntu, “may I not be”: the perfect after lā is a wish or curse, here directed at oneself. yaṭraḥu, “throws”, has no object; “throws himself down”, i.e. yields, is the likeliest sense, but the word is unusual here and may be corrupt. The three gifts end alike in -ī (janāḥī, nafsī, ʿaynī), a small run of rhyme.

sentences.t: وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ مَنْ تَشَبَّهَ بِأَقْوَى مِنْهُ تَعِبَ وَرُبَّمَا هَلَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-iʿlam anna man tashabbaha bi-aqwā minhu taʿiba wa-rubbamā halaka
sentences.l: And know that whoever likened-himself to-one-stronger than-him toiled, and perhaps perished.
sentences.i: And know that whoever tries to ape one stronger than himself comes to grief, and may well perish.
sentences.n: tashabbaha bi-, “to make oneself like, imitate”: the verb chooses bi-. rubbamā, “perhaps, sometimes”. The shadda in تشبّه is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا أَخَافُ عَلَيْكَ إِنْ تَشَبَّهْتَ بِمَنْ هُوَ أَقْوَى مِنْكَ أَنْ يَجْرِيَ لَكَ مَا جَرَى لِلْعُصْفُورِ
sentences.tr: wa-anā akhāfu ʿalayka in tashabbahta bi-man huwa aqwā minka an yajriya laka mā jarā li-al-ʿuṣfūri
sentences.l: And I fear for-you, if you-liken-yourself to-one-who he (is) stronger than-you, that there-happen to-you what happened to-the sparrow.
sentences.i: I fear that if you try to ape one stronger than you, the same will happen to you as happened to the sparrow.”
sentences.n: khāfa ʿalā, “to fear for (someone)”; jarā li-, “to happen to”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الثَّعْلَبُ وَأَيُّ شَيْءٍ جَرَى لِلْعُصْفُورِ فَبِاللَّهِ عَلَيْكَ أَنْ تُحَدِّثَنِي بِحَدِيثِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-thaʿlabu wa-ayyu shayʾin jarā li-al-ʿuṣfūri fa-bi-Allāhi ʿalayka an tuḥaddithanī bi-ḥadīthihi
sentences.l: And the fox said to-him: And what thing happened to-the sparrow? So by-God (be it) upon-you that you-tell-me his-story.
sentences.i: The fox said to him, “And what happened to the sparrow? By God, I beg you, tell me his story.”
sentences.n: bi-Allāhi ʿalayka, “by God (I lay it) upon you”, is a common form of entreaty. ḥaddatha bi-, “to tell (a story)”: the verb chooses bi-.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْغُرَابُ بَلَغَنِي أَنَّ عُصْفُورًا كَانَ طَائِرًا بِمُرَاحِ غَنَمٍ فَنَظَرَ إِلَى هَذَا الْمُرَاحِ وَوَقَفَ يَتَأَمَّلُ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ghurābu balaghanī anna ʿuṣfūran kāna ṭāʾiran bi-murāḥi ghanamin fa-naẓara ilā hādhā al-murāḥi wa-waqafa yataʾammalu fīhi
sentences.l: And the crow said: It-has-reached-me that a sparrow was flying at a fold of sheep; and he-looked at this fold and stopped, contemplating it.
sentences.i: The crow said: “I have heard that a sparrow was once flying over a sheepfold. He looked down at the fold and stopped to watch it.
sentences.n: The crow opens his fable with balaghanī, “it has reached me”, the same words Shahrazād uses for her own tales; the print sets it on a line by itself. murāḥ, “the fold where flocks are penned at night”. taʾammala fī, “to gaze at, consider”.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِعُقَابٍ كَبِيرٍ انْقَضَّ عَلَى رَمِيسٍ مِنْ صِغَارِ أَوْلَادِ الْغَنَمِ فَاخْتَطَفَهُ بَيْنَ مَخَالِبِهِ وَطَارَ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-ʿuqābin kabīrin inqaḍḍa ʿalā ramīsin min ṣighāri awlādi al-ghanami fa-ikhtaṭafahu bayna makhālibihi wa-ṭāra
sentences.l: And behold, a great eagle swooped upon a ramīs from the small ones of the young of the sheep, and snatched-it between his-talons and flew.
sentences.i: And all at once a great eagle swooped down on a lamb, one of the little ones of the flock, snatched it up in its talons and flew off.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-, “and behold”: the bi- only marks what appears. inqaḍḍa ʿalā, “to swoop down on”; the shadda in انقضّ is the print's own. ʿuqāb, “eagle”, is usually feminine; here it takes masculine forms. ramīs is obscure: the sense is plainly a lamb or kid, “of the little ones of the flock”, but no such word for a young animal is known to the lexicons, and the letters may be corrupt. It is kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأٰهُ الْعُصْفُورُ رَفْرَفَ بِجَنَاحِهِ وَقَالَ أَنَا أَفْعَلُ مِثْلَ مَا فَعَلَ هَذَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhu al-ʿuṣfūru rafrafa bi-janāḥihi wa-qāla anā afʿalu mithla mā faʿala hādhā
sentences.l: And when the sparrow saw-him, he-fluttered with-his-wing and said: I will-do like what this-one did.
sentences.i: When the sparrow saw it, he flapped his wings and said, ‘I will do just what that one did.’

sentences.t: وَأَعْجَبَتْهُ نَفْسُهُ وَتَشَبَّهَ بِمَنْ هُوَ أَكْبَرُ مِنْهُ فَطَارَ لِوَقْتِهِ وَانْقَضَّ عَلَى كَبْشٍ سَمِينٍ لَهُ صُوفٌ كَثِيرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-aʿjabathu nafsuhu wa-tashabbaha bi-man huwa akbaru minhu fa-ṭāra li-waqtihi wa-inqaḍḍa ʿalā kabshin samīnin lahu ṣūfun kathīrun
sentences.l: And his-self pleased-him, and he-likened-himself to-one-who he (is) bigger than-him; so he-flew at-his-moment and swooped upon a fat ram to-which (was) much wool.
sentences.i: He was pleased with himself, and set out to ape one bigger than he: at once he flew up and swooped down on a fat ram with a heavy fleece.
sentences.n: aʿjabathu nafsuhu, “his self pleased him”: he was full of himself. li-waqtihi, “at that very moment”: li- marks the time. The shadda in انقضّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ تَلَبَّدَ صُوفُهُ مِنْ رُقَادِهِ عَلَى بَوْلِهِ وَرَوْثِهِ فَصَارَ صُوفُهُ مِثْلَ الْبُزَاقِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad talabbada ṣūfuhu min ruqādihi ʿalā bawlihi wa-rawthihi fa-ṣāra ṣūfuhu mithla al-buzāqi
sentences.l: And had matted his-wool from his-lying upon his-urine and his-dung, so became his-wool like the spittle.
sentences.i: Its wool had matted from lying in its own urine and dung, until the fleece was as sticky as spittle.
sentences.n: talabbada, “to become matted, felted”. ruqād, “sleep, lying down”. buzāq, “spittle”, a by-form of buṣāq: the fleece was gummy and clinging.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا انْقَضَّ عَلَى ظَهْرِهِ صَفَقَ بِجَنَاحَيْهِ فَاشْتَبَكَتْ رِجْلَاهُ فِى الصُّوفِ فَأَرَادَ أَنْ يَطِيرَ فَلَمْ يَسْتَطِعْ أَنْ يُخَلِّصَ نَفْسَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā inqaḍḍa ʿalā ẓahrihi ṣafaqa bi-janāḥayhi fa-ishtabakat rijlāhu fī al-ṣūfi fa-arāda an yaṭīra fa-lam yastaṭiʿ an yukhalliṣa nafsahu
sentences.l: And when he-swooped upon its-back, he-clapped with-his-two-wings, and his-two-feet became-entangled in the wool; and he-wanted to fly, but he-could-not free himself.
sentences.i: When he landed on its back he beat his wings, and his feet were caught fast in the wool; he tried to fly off, but he could not free himself.
sentences.n: ṣafaqa bi-janāḥayhi, “to beat (with) his wings”: bi- marks the instrument. ishtabaka, “to become entangled”. The print writes fī with ى here.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ حَصَلَ كُلُّ هَذَا وَالرَّاعِي يَنْظُرُ مَاجَرَي مِنَ الْعُقَابِ أَوَّلًا وَمَاجَرَى لِلْعُصْفُورِ ثَانِيًا
sentences.tr: wa-qad ḥaṣala kullu hādhā wa-al-rāʿī yanẓuru mā jarā mina al-ʿuqābi awwalan wa-mā jarā li-al-ʿuṣfūri thāniyan
sentences.l: And all this had happened while the shepherd (was) watching what happened from the eagle first, and what happened to-the sparrow second.
sentences.i: All this time the shepherd had been watching: first what the eagle did, then what befell the sparrow.
sentences.n: wa-al-rāʿī yanẓuru, “while the shepherd watched”: a circumstantial clause with wa-. The print runs mā jarā together both times, spelling it once with ي and once with ى. min al-ʿuqāb, “from the eagle”, is what the eagle did; li-al-ʿuṣfūr, “to the sparrow”, what was done to him. The shadda in اوّلا is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَجَاءَ الرَّاعِي إِلَى الْعُصْفُورِ غَضْبَانًا فَقَبَضَهُ وَنَتَفَ رِيشَ أَجْنِحَتِهِ وَرَبَطَ فِي رِجْلَيْهِ خَيْطًا وَأَتَى بِهِ إِلَى أَوْلَادِهِ وَرَمَاهُ لَهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-jāʾa al-rāʿī ilā al-ʿuṣfūri ghaḍbānan fa-qabaḍahu wa-natafa rīsha ajniḥatihi wa-rabaṭa fī rijlayhi khayṭan wa-atā bihi ilā awlādihi wa-ramāhu lahum
sentences.l: And the shepherd came to the sparrow angry, and seized-him, and plucked the feathers of his-wings, and tied on his-two-feet a thread, and brought him to his-children and threw-him to-them.
sentences.i: The shepherd came over to the sparrow in a rage, caught him, plucked the feathers from his wings, tied a string to his feet, and took him to his children and tossed him to them.
sentences.n: ghaḍbānan, “angry”: Classical Arabic treats ghaḍbān as a diptote (ghaḍbāna), but the print gives it the full tanwīn alif, as everyday Arabic did. qabaḍahu, “seized him”, takes a direct object here, where Classical usage prefers qabaḍa ʿalā. atā bi-, “to bring”: the verb chooses bi-.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ بَعْضُ الْأَوْلَادِ مَا هَذَا فَقَالَ هَذَا تَشَبَّهَ بِمَنْ هُوَ أَعْلَى مِنْهُ فَهَلَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla baʿḍu al-awlādi mā hādhā fa-qāla hādhā tashabbaha bi-man huwa aʿlā minhu fa-halaka
sentences.l: And some of the children said: What (is) this? And he-said: This-one likened-himself to-one-who he (is) higher than-him, and perished.
sentences.i: One of the children asked, ‘What is this?’ and he answered, ‘This one tried to ape his betters, and it was the end of him.’
sentences.n: The shadda in تشبّه is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَأَنْتَ كَذَلِكَ أَيُّهَا الثَّعْلَبُ أُحَذِّرُكَ أَنْ تَتَشَبَّهَ بِمَنْ هُوَ أَقْوَي مِنْكَ فَتَهْلِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-anta ka-dhālika ayyuhā al-thaʿlabu uḥadhdhiruka an tatashabbaha bi-man huwa aqwā minka fa-tahlika
sentences.l: And you (are) like-that, O you the fox: I-warn-you against that you-liken-yourself to-one-who he (is) stronger than-you, and so perish.
sentences.i: And so with you, fox: I warn you not to ape one stronger than you, or you will perish.
sentences.n: ḥadhdhara, “to warn”, here with an an-clause, “warn against doing”. fa-tahlika is subjunctive, joined to an tatashabbaha. The print spells aqwā with a dotted ي (اقوي). The shadda in تتشبّه is the print's own.

sentences.t: هَذَا مَا عِنْدِى مِنَ الْكَلَامِ فَاذْهَبْ عَنِّي بِسَلَامٍ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā ʿindī mina al-kalāmi fa-idhhab ʿannī bi-salāmin
sentences.l: This (is) what (is) with-me of the speech; so go from-me in-peace.
sentences.i: That is all I have to say. Now go away and leave me in peace.”
sentences.n: kalām / salām: the crow signs off in rhyme. bi-salām, “in peace”: bi- of manner. The print writes ʿindī with ى.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا يَئِسَ الثَّعْلَبُ مِنْ مُصَادَقَةِ الْغُرَابِ رَجَعَ مِنْ حُزْنِهِ يَئِنُّ وَقَرَعَ لِلنَّدَامَةِ سِنًّا عَلَى سِنٍّ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā yaʾisa al-thaʿlabu min muṣādaqati al-ghurābi rajaʿa min ḥuznihi yaʾinnu wa-qaraʿa li-al-nadāmati sinnan ʿalā sinnin
sentences.l: And when the fox despaired of the befriending of the crow, he-turned-back from his-grief moaning, and he-knocked for-the remorse tooth upon tooth.
sentences.i: When the fox gave up hope of the crow's friendship, he turned away moaning with grief, and ground his teeth in regret.
sentences.n: yaʾisa min, “to despair of”. yaʾinnu, “moaning”, a circumstantial verb; its kasra, fatḥa and shadda are the print's own. qaraʿa sinnan ʿalā sinnin, “struck tooth on tooth”, the gesture of remorse: li-al-nadāma, “for regret”, gives the cause.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْغُرَابُ بُكَاءً وَأَنَّهُ وَرَأَى كَآبَتَهُ وَحُزْنَهُ قَالَ أَيُّهَا الثَّعْلَبُ مَا نَابَكَ حَتَّي قَرَعْتَ نَابَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-ghurābu bukāʾan wa-annahu wa-raʾā kaʾābatahu wa-ḥuznahu qāla ayyuhā al-thaʿlabu mā nābaka ḥattā qaraʿta nābaka
sentences.l: And when the crow heard weeping and his-moaning, and saw his-dejection and his-grief, he-said: O you the fox, what has-befallen-you that you-have-knocked your-canine-tooth?
sentences.i: When the crow heard the weeping and moaning and saw how downcast and grieved he was, he said, “Fox, what has befallen you, that you gnash your fangs?”
sentences.n: annahu here is not the conjunction anna but the verbal noun ann, “moaning” (from anna, yaʾinnu, as in the last sentence), with -hu, “his”; the shadda is the print's own. bukāʾan has no pronoun in the print, and reads as “weeping” in general. mā nābaka … nābaka is a pun: the first nāba is the verb “to befall”, the second nāb the canine tooth. The print spells ḥattā with ي.

sentences.t: قَالَ لَهُ الثَّعْلَبُ إِنَّمَا قَرَعْتُ سِنِّي لِأَنِّي رَأَيْتُكَ أَخْدَعَ مِنِّي
sentences.tr: qāla lahu al-thaʿlabu innamā qaraʿtu sinnī li-annī raʾaytuka akhdaʿa minnī
sentences.l: The fox said to-him: Only I-knocked my-tooth because I saw-you more-cunning than-me.
sentences.i: The fox answered, “I gnash my teeth only because I see that you are craftier than I am.”
sentences.n: innamā, “only, it is only that”. akhdaʿ, “more deceitful, wilier”, the elative of khadaʿa. The shaddas in انّما and سنّي are the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ وَلَّى هَارِبًا وَرَدَّ رَاجِعًا وَلِجُحْرِهِ طَالِبًا
sentences.tr: thumma innahu wallā hāriban wa-radda rājiʿan wa-li-juḥrihi ṭāliban
sentences.l: Then he turned-away fleeing, and went-back returning, and for-his-hole seeking.
sentences.i: Then he turned tail and fled, and went back the way he came, making for his den.
sentences.n: Three accusatives of state in rhyme, hāriban, rājiʿan, ṭāliban. li-juḥrihi ṭāliban, “seeking his burrow”: the li- marks the object of the participle placed before it. The shadda in ولّى is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَهَذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ حَدِيثِهِمَا أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā mā kāna min ḥadīthihimā ayyuhā al-maliku
sentences.l: And this (is) what was of the story of-the-two-of-them, O you the king.
sentences.i: And that, O king, is the story of those two.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ يَا شَهْرَزَادُ مَا أَحْسَنَ هَذِهِ الْحِكَايَاتِ وَأَطْيَبَهَا هَلْ عِنْدَكِ شَيْءٌ مِثْلُهَا مِنَ الْمَوْعِظَاتِ قَالَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-maliku yā Shahrazādu mā aḥsana hādhihi al-ḥikāyāti wa-aṭyabahā hal ʿindaki shayʾun mithluhā mina al-mawʿiẓāti qālat
sentences.l: And the king said: O Shahrazād, how beautiful (are) these tales, and how-pleasant-they-are! Is there with-you a thing like-them of the admonitions? She-said:
sentences.i: The king said, “Shahrazād, how fine these tales are, and how delightful! Do you have any more like them, tales with a moral?” She said:
sentences.n: mā aḥsana …, “how fine is …!”: the verb of wonder, with its object in the accusative; wa-aṭyabahā repeats the pattern. mawʿiẓāt, plural of mawʿiẓa, “admonition, edifying lesson”. ḥikāyāt / mawʿiẓāt rhyme. Her answer begins the next part of the night.

sentences.t: وَيُحْكَى أَنَّ قُنْفُذًا اتَّخَذَ مَسْكَنًا بِجَانِبِ نَخْلَةٍ وَكَانَ قَدْ أَلِفَهَا الْوَرَشَانُ وَزَوْجَتُهُ وَعَشَّشَا فِيهَا وَسَكَنَا بِهَا فِي عَيْشٍ رَغِيدٍ
sentences.tr: wa-yuḥkā anna qunfudhan ittakhadha maskanan bi-jānibi nakhlatin wa-kāna qad alifahā al-warashānu wa-zawjatuhu wa-ʿashshashā fīhā wa-sakanā bihā fī ʿayshin raghīdin
sentences.l: And it-is-told that a hedgehog took a dwelling beside a palm-tree; and the ringdove and his-wife had grown-familiar-with it, and the-two nested in-it and the-two dwelt in-it in a life easy-and-plentiful.
sentences.i: And it is told that a hedgehog made his home beside a palm-tree. A ringdove and his mate had long made that palm their haunt; they had built their nest in it and lived there in ease and plenty.
sentences.n: A new fable begins. qunfudh, “hedgehog”. warashān, “ringdove, wood-pigeon” (Lane); the bird is masculine and his mate is his zawja, “wife”. alifa, “to become familiar with, keep to a place”. ʿashshasha, “to build a nest” (from ʿushsh, “nest”), dual here. ʿaysh raghīd, “an easy, abundant life”. The shaddas in انّ, اتّخذ and عشّشا are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْقُنْفُذُ فِي نَفْسِهِ إِنَّ الْوَرَشَانَ وَزَوْجَتَهُ يَأْكُلَانِ مِنْ ثَمَرِ النَّخْلَةِ وَأَنَا لَا أَجِدُ إِلَي ذَلِكَ سَبِيلًا وَلَكِنْ لَابُدَّ مِنِ اسْتِعْمَالِ الْحِيلَةِ عَلَيْهِمَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-qunfudhu fī nafsihi inna al-warashāna wa-zawjatahu yaʾkulāni min thamari al-nakhlati wa-anā lā ajidu ilā dhālika sabīlan wa-lākin lā budda mini istiʿmāli al-ḥīlati ʿalayhimā
sentences.l: And the hedgehog said in his-soul: Indeed the ringdove and his-wife eat-(the-two) from the fruit of the palm, and I, I-do-not find to that a way; but there-is-no escape from the using of the trick upon-them-two.
sentences.i: The hedgehog said to himself, “The ringdove and his mate feed on the fruit of the palm, and I can find no way to it. There is nothing for it but to work some trick on the pair of them.”
sentences.n: fī nafsihi, “in his soul”, i.e. to himself. lā ajidu ilā dhālika sabīlan, “I find no road to that”. The print writes ilā as الي, with ي for the final alif, as it often does with ʿalā (علي) and ḥattā (حتي); this is the edition's spelling habit and is kept. lābudda, “there is no escape”, i.e. “it must be”, is printed as one word. ḥīla, “stratagem, trick”; istiʿmāl al-ḥīla ʿalā, “using a trick against”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ حَفَرَ فِي أَسْفَلِ النَّخْلَةِ بَيْتًا وَاتَّخَذَهُ مَسْكَنًا لَهُ وَلِزَوْجَتِهِ وَاتَّخَذَ جَانِبَهُ مَسْجِدًا وَانْفَرَدَ فِيهِ وَأَظْهَرَ النُّسْكَ وَالْعِبَادَةَ وَتَرَكَ الدُّنْيَا
sentences.tr: thumma ḥafara fī asfali al-nakhlati baytan wa-ittakhadhahu maskanan lahu wa-li-zawjatihi wa-ittakhadha jānibahu masjidan wa-infarada fīhi wa-aẓhara al-nuska wa-al-ʿibādata wa-taraka al-dunyā
sentences.l: Then he-dug in the bottom of the palm a house, and took-it (as) a dwelling for-him and for-his-wife; and he-took (at) its-side a place-of-prostration, and withdrew-alone in-it, and made-show-of the asceticism and the worship, and left the world.
sentences.i: Then he dug a burrow at the foot of the palm and made it a home for himself and his wife. Beside it he set up a place of prayer, where he withdrew alone; he made a show of piety and devotion and renounced the world.
sentences.n: masjid, literally “place of prostration”, here simply the hedgehog's prayer-nook. infarada, “to withdraw, be alone”. aẓhara, “to show, display”: the verb is the fable's point, for the piety is put on. nusk, “devout practice, asceticism”. al-dunyā, “the world”, the life of this world as against the hereafter.

sentences.t: فَكَانَ الْوَرَشَانُ يَرَاهُ مُتَعَبِّدًا مُصَلِّيًا فَرَقَّ لَهُ مِنْ شِدَّةِ زُهْدِهِ وَقٰلَ لَهُ كَمْ سَنَةً وَأَنْتَ هَكَذَا
sentences.tr: fa-kāna al-warashānu yarāhu mutaʿabbidan muṣalliyan fa-raqqa lahu min shiddati zuhdihi wa-qāla lahu kam sanatan wa-anta hākadhā
sentences.l: And the ringdove used-to see-him worshipping, praying; and he-grew-tender toward-him from the intensity of his-renunciation, and said to-him: How-many a-year (have you been) and you (are) thus?
sentences.i: The ringdove would see him at his devotions and his prayers, and his heart went out to him for the strictness of his renunciation. He said to him, “How many years have you lived like this?”
sentences.n: raqqa li-, “to soften toward, feel for”: the verb chooses li- (la- before a pronoun, as in lahu). zuhd, “renunciation of the world”. The print spells qāla defectively as قل; the dagger alif restores the long vowel without changing the letters. kam sanatan, “how many years”: kam takes an accusative singular noun. wa-anta hākadhā, “while you are thus”, a circumstantial clause.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ مِنْ مُدَّةِ ثَلٰثِينَ سَنَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla min muddati thalāthīna sanatan
sentences.l: And he-said: From a space of thirty years.
sentences.i: He said, “For thirty years now.”
sentences.n: The print writes thirty as ثلثين, without its medial alif; the dagger alif marks the ā. min muddati, “since a span of”.

sentences.t: قَالَ مَا طَعَامُكَ قَالَ مَا يَسْقُطُ مِنَ النَّخْلَةِ
sentences.tr: qāla mā ṭaʿāmuka qāla mā yasquṭu mina al-nakhlati
sentences.l: He-said: What (is) your-food? He-said: What falls from the palm.
sentences.i: “And what do you eat?” “Whatever falls from the palm.”
sentences.n: Two different mā: the first asks “what?”, the second is the relative “that which”.

sentences.t: قَالَ مَا لِبَاسُكَ قَالَ شَوْكٌ أَنْتَفِعُ بِخُشُونَتِهِ
sentences.tr: qāla mā libāsuka qāla shawkun antafiʿu bi-khushūnatihi
sentences.l: He-said: What (is) your-clothing? He-said: Thorns; I-profit by its-roughness.
sentences.i: “And what do you wear?” “Thorns; their roughness does me good.”
sentences.n: shawk, “thorns, spines”: the hedgehog's own quills, passed off as a hair shirt. intafaʿa bi-, “to benefit from”: the verb chooses bi-. khushūna, “roughness, coarseness”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ وَكَيْفَ اخْتَرْتَ مَكَانَكَ هَذَا عَلَي غَيْرِهِ قَالَ اخْتَرْتُهُ عَلَي غَيْرِ طَرِيقٍ لِأَجْلِ أَنْ أُرْشِدَ الضَّالَّ وَأُعَلِّمَ الْجَاهِلَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla wa-kayfa ikhtarta makānaka hādhā ʿalā ghayrihi qāla ikhtartuhu ʿalā ghayri ṭarīqin li-ajli an urshida al-ḍālla wa-uʿallima al-jāhila
sentences.l: And he-said: And how (did) you-choose this your-place over other-than-it? He-said: I-chose-it off any road, for-the-sake-of that I-may-guide the straying and teach the ignorant.
sentences.i: He said, “And why did you choose this place of yours over any other?” He said, “I chose it away from the beaten road, so that I might guide the one who has lost his way and teach the ignorant.”
sentences.n: ikhtāra … ʿalā, “to choose … over”. ʿalā ghayri ṭarīqin is not quite clear: most likely “off any road”, out where travellers stray, which suits guiding al-ḍāll, “the one who has gone astray”; it could also mean “by no set path”. The print's علي is ʿalā written with ي. li-ajli an, “for the sake of, so that”, with the subjunctive. ḍāll / jāhil, “the strayed / the ignorant”, end the reply on a jingle.

sentences.t: قَالَ لَهُ الْوَرَشَانُ كُنْتُ أَظُنُّ أَنَّكَ عَلَي غَيْرِ هَذِهِ الْحَالَةِ وَلَكِنِّي الْآنَ رَغِبْتُ فِيمَا عِنْدَكَ
sentences.tr: qāla lahu al-warashānu kuntu aẓunnu annaka ʿalā ghayri hādhihi al-ḥālati wa-lākinnī al-āna raghibtu fīmā ʿindaka
sentences.l: The ringdove said to-him: I-was thinking that you (were) upon other-than this state; but-I now have-come-to-desire what (is) with-you.
sentences.i: The ringdove said to him, “I used to think you were otherwise than this; but now I long for what you have.”
sentences.n: kuntu aẓunnu, “I used to think”. raghiba fī, “to desire, long for”: the verb chooses fī. fīmā ʿindaka, “in what is with you”, i.e. your way of life.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْقُنْفُذُ إِنِّي أَخْشَي أَنْ يَكُونَ قَوْلُكَ ضِدَّ فِعْلِكَ فَتَكُونَ كَالزَّرَّاعِ الَّذِي لَمَّا جَاءَ وَقْتُ الزَّرْعِ قَصَّرَ فِي بَذْرِهِ وَقَالَ إِنِّي أَخْشَي أَنْ لَا تُبَلِّغَنِي الْأَيَّامُ أُمْنِيَّتِي فَأَكُونَ قَدْ بَدَأْتُ بِإِضَاعَةِ الْمَالِ وَسُرْعَةِ الْبَذْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-qunfudhu innī akhshā an yakūna qawluka ḍidda fiʿlika fa-takūna ka-al-zarrāʿi alladhī lammā jāʾa waqtu al-zarʿi qaṣṣara fī badhrihi wa-qāla innī akhshā an lā tuballighanī al-ayyāmu umniyyatī fa-akūna qad badaʾtu bi-iḍāʿati al-māli wa-surʿati al-badhri
sentences.l: And the hedgehog said: I fear that your-saying be the opposite of your-doing, and you-be like-the sower who, when the time of the sowing came, fell-short in his-seeding, and said: I fear that the days will-not bring-me-to my-wish, and I-shall-be (one who) has begun with the wasting of the wealth and the haste of the seed.
sentences.i: The hedgehog said, “I fear your words may run contrary to your deeds, and you will be like the farmer who, when sowing-time came, held back his seed. He said, ‘I fear the days may not bring me to what I hope for, and then I shall only have begun by squandering my money and rushing my seed into the ground.’
sentences.n: ka-al-zarrāʿ: ka-, “like”, governs the noun; zarrāʿ, “sower, farmer”. qaṣṣara fī, “to fall short in, stint”. The print writes akhshā, “I fear”, with ي for the final alif. ballagha, “to make reach”: an lā tuballighanī al-ayyāmu umniyyatī, “that the days will not bring me to my wish”. bi-iḍāʿati: bi-, “with”, chosen by badaʾa, “to begin with”. The farmer's fear is that seed sown is money thrown away if he does not live to reap.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا جَاءَ وَقْتُ الْحَصَادِ وَرَأَى النَّاسَ وَهُمْ يَحْصُدُونَ نَدِمَ عَلَي مَافَاتَهُ مِنْ تَخَلُّفِهِ وَمَاتَ أَسَفًا وَحُزْنًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā jāʾa waqtu al-ḥaṣādi wa-raʾā al-nāsa wa-hum yaḥṣudūna nadima ʿalā mā fātahu min takhallufihi wa-māta asafan wa-ḥuznan
sentences.l: And when the time of the harvest came, and he-saw the people while they (were) reaping, he-regretted what had-escaped-him from his-lagging-behind, and died (of) sorrow and grief.
sentences.i: And when harvest-time came and he saw the people reaping, he rued what his hanging back had cost him, and died of sorrow and grief.’
sentences.n: nadima ʿalā, “to regret”: the verb chooses ʿalā. The print runs mā fātahu, “what had escaped him”, together as مافاته. takhalluf, “staying behind, failing to act”. asafan wa-ḥuznan, accusatives of cause: “out of sorrow and grief”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْوَرَشَانُ لِلْقُنْفُذِ وَمَاذَا أَصْنَعُ حَتَّي أَتَخَلَّصَ مِنْ عَلَائِقِ الدُّنْيَا وَأَنْقَطِعَ إِلَى عِبَادَةِ رَبِّي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-warashānu li-al-qunfudhi wa-mādhā aṣnaʿu ḥattā atakhallaṣa min ʿalāʾiqi al-dunyā wa-anqaṭiʿa ilā ʿibādati rabbī
sentences.l: And the ringdove said to-the hedgehog: And what shall-I-do so-that I-may-get-free from the attachments of the world and cut-myself-off to the worship of my-Lord?
sentences.i: The ringdove said to the hedgehog, “Then what must I do to free myself from the ties of this world and give myself wholly to the worship of my Lord?”
sentences.n: li-al-qunfudh: li-, “to”, marks the one addressed. ʿalāʾiq, plural of ʿalāqa, “ties, attachments”. inqaṭaʿa ilā, “to cut oneself off (from all else) for”, i.e. devote oneself entirely to.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْقُنْفُذُ خُذْ فِى الِاسْتِعْدَادِ لِلْمَعَادِ وَالْقَنَاعَةِ بِالْكَفَافِ مِنَ الزَّادِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-qunfudhu khudh fī al-istiʿdādi li-al-maʿādi wa-al-qanāʿati bi-al-kafāfi mina al-zādi
sentences.l: And the hedgehog said to-him: Take-to the preparing for-the Return, and the contentment with-the bare-sufficiency of the provision.
sentences.i: The hedgehog said to him, “Set about making ready for the Return, and be content with just enough provision to live on.”
sentences.n: akhadha fī, “to set about, begin”: khudh fī is its imperative. maʿād, “the place of return”, the life to come. li- marks what one prepares for; bi- after qanāʿa, “contentment with”, is chosen by the noun. The rhyme falls on maʿād / zād. The print writes fī here with ى.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْوَرَشَانُ كَيْفَ لِي بِذَلِكَ وَأَنَا طَائِرٌ لَا أَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ أَتَجَاوَزَ النَّخْلَةَ الَّتِي فِيهَا قُوتِي وَلَوِ اسْتَطَعْتُ ذَلِكَ مَا عَرَفْتُ مَوْضِعًا أَسْتَقِرُّ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-warashānu kayfa lī bi-dhālika wa-anā ṭāʾirun lā astaṭīʿu an atajāwaza al-nakhlata allatī fīhā qūtī wa-lawi istaṭaʿtu dhālika mā ʿaraftu mawḍiʿan astaqirru fīhi
sentences.l: And the ringdove said: How (is it) for-me with that, and I (am) a bird; I-cannot pass-beyond the palm in-which (is) my-food; and if I-could-do that, I-would-not-know a place I-could-settle in-it.
sentences.i: The ringdove said, “How can I manage that? I am a bird; I cannot go beyond the palm that holds my food, and even if I could, I would know of no place to settle.”
sentences.n: kayfa lī bi-…, “how can I come by …”: bi- marks the thing one cannot get. law … mā …, “if … I would not …”, with the negated perfect in the answer clause.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْقُنْفُذُ يُمْكِنُكَ أَنْ تَنْثُرَ مِنْ ثَمَرِ النَّخْلَةِ مَا يَكْفِيكَ مُؤْنَةَ عَامٍ أَنْتَ وَزَوْجَتُكَ وَتَسْكُنَ فِي وَكْرٍ تَحْتَ النَّخْلَةِ لِالْتِمَاسِ حُسْنِ إِرْشَادِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-qunfudhu yumkinuka an tanthura min thamari al-nakhlati mā yakfīka muʾnata ʿāmin anta wa-zawjatuka wa-taskuna fī wakrin taḥta al-nakhlati li-iltimāsi ḥusni irshādika
sentences.l: And the hedgehog said: It-is-possible-for-you that you-scatter of the fruit of the palm what suffices-you (for) the provision of a year, you and your-wife, and dwell in a nest under the palm, for-the seeking of the goodness of your-guidance.
sentences.i: The hedgehog said, “You can shake down from the palm as much fruit as will keep you and your wife for a year, and live in a nest under the palm, so as to seek right guidance for yourself.
sentences.n: nathara, “to scatter, shake down”. muʾna, “provision, supplies”; muʾnata ʿāmin, “a year's supply”. wakr, “nest”, also used of a burrow. li-iltimāsi: li-, “for, in order to”, + iltimās, “seeking”. ḥusn irshādika, “the goodness of your guidance”, is loose: read “to seek good guidance for yourself”, or perhaps “to seek out my good guidance”. The text says only what is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مِلْ إِلَى مَا نَثَرْتَهُ مِنَ الثَّمَرِ فَانْقُلْهُ جَمِيعَهُ وَادَّخِرْهُ قُوتًا لِلْعَدَمِ
sentences.tr: thumma mil ilā mā nathartahu mina al-thamari fa-inqulhu jamīʿahu wa-iddakhirhu qūtan li-al-ʿadami
sentences.l: Then turn to what you-have-scattered of the fruit, and carry-it all-of-it, and store-it (as) food for-the want.
sentences.i: Then go to the fruit you have shaken down, carry it all off, and lay it up as food against the time of want.
sentences.n: mil, “turn, incline”, imperative of māla; the kasra and sukūn on مِلْ are the print's own. iddakhara, “to store up”. li-al-ʿadam: li-, “for, against”, + ʿadam, “lack, want”.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا فَرَغَتِ الثِّمَارُ وَطَالَ عَلَيْكَ الْمِطَالُ صِرْ إِلَى كَفَافٍ مِنَ الْعَيْشِ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā faraghati al-thimāru wa-ṭāla ʿalayka al-miṭālu ṣir ilā kafāfin mina al-ʿayshi
sentences.l: And when the fruits run-out and the putting-off grows-long upon-you, go to a bare-sufficiency of the living.
sentences.i: And when the fruit runs out and the waiting grows long for you, come down to a bare sufficiency of living.
sentences.n: faragha, “to come to an end, run out”. miṭāl, “putting off, delay”, verbal noun of māṭala; ṭāla … al-miṭāl is a jingle of sound only: ṭāla is from ṭ-w-l, “long”, miṭāl from m-ṭ-l, “to put off”. ṣir, “become, go over to”, imperative of ṣāra.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْوَرَشَانُ جَزَاكَ اللَّهُ خَيْرًا بِحُسْنِ النِّيَّةِ حَيْثُ ذَكَّرْتَنِي بِالْمَعَادِ وَهَدَيْتَنِي إِلَى الرَّشَادِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-warashānu jazāka Allāhu khayran bi-ḥusni al-niyyati ḥaythu dhakkartanī bi-al-maʿādi wa-hadaytanī ilā al-rashādi
sentences.l: And the ringdove said: May-God reward-you (with) good for the goodness of the intention, since you-reminded-me of-the Return and guided-me to the right-way.
sentences.i: The ringdove said, “God reward you well for your good intent, for you have reminded me of the Return and guided me to the right path.”
sentences.n: jazāka allāhu khayran, “may God repay you with good”, the ordinary formula of thanks. bi-ḥusni: bi-, “for, in return for”. dhakkara bi-, “to remind of”: the verb chooses bi-. The rhyme maʿād / rashād.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَعِبَ الْوَرَشَانُ وَزَوْجَتُهُ فِي طَرْحِ الثَّمَرِ حَتَّى لَمْ يَبْقَ فِى النَّخْلَةِ شَيْءٌ
sentences.tr: thumma taʿiba al-warashānu wa-zawjatuhu fī ṭarḥi al-thamari ḥattā lam yabqa fī al-nakhlati shayʾun
sentences.l: Then the ringdove and his-wife toiled in the throwing-down of the fruit until there-did-not remain in the palm a thing.
sentences.i: Then the ringdove and his mate toiled at casting down the fruit until there was nothing left in the palm.
sentences.n: taʿiba fī, “to labour at”. ṭarḥ, “throwing down”. The verb taʿiba is singular before its compound subject, as usual when the verb comes first.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدَ الْقُنْفُذُ مَا يَأْكُلُ وَفَرِحَ بِهِ وَمَلَأَ مَسْكَنَهُ مِنَ الثَّمَرِ وَادَّخَرَهُ لِقُوتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-wajada al-qunfudhu mā yaʾkulu wa-fariḥa bihi wa-malaʾa maskanahu mina al-thamari wa-iddakharahu li-qūtihi
sentences.l: And the hedgehog found what he-might-eat, and rejoiced in-it, and filled his-dwelling with the fruit, and stored-it for-his-food.
sentences.i: So the hedgehog found something to eat. He was glad of it, filled his home with the fruit, and laid it up for his own keep.
sentences.n: fariḥa bi-, “to rejoice at”: the verb chooses bi-. li-qūtihi: li-, “for”, purpose.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ إِنَّ الْوَرَشَانَ هُوَ وَزَوْجَتُهُ إِذَا احْتَاجَا إِلَى مُؤْنَتِهِمَا طَلَبَاهَا مِنِّي وَطَمِعَا فِيمَا عِنْدِي وَرَكَنَا إِلَى تَزَهُّدِي وَوَرَعِي
sentences.tr: wa-qāla fī nafsihi inna al-warashāna huwa wa-zawjatuhu idhā iḥtājā ilā muʾnatihimā ṭalabāhā minnī wa-ṭamiʿā fīmā ʿindī wa-rakanā ilā tazahhudī wa-waraʿī
sentences.l: And he-said in his-soul: Indeed the ringdove, he and his-wife, when they-two-need their-provision, will-seek-it from-me and covet what (is) with-me, and lean on my-show-of-renunciation and my-scrupulousness.
sentences.i: And he said to himself, “When the ringdove and his mate come to need their stores, they will ask them of me and set their hopes on what I have, and they will trust my abstinence and my scruples.
sentences.n: inna al-warashāna huwa wa-zawjatuhu: the topic is stated, then picked up by huwa so that the wife can be added. iḥtāja ilā, “to need”. ṭamiʿa fī, “to covet, set one's hopes on”. rakana ilā, “to lean on, trust”. tazahhud, “practising renunciation”, the form V that often means putting it on; waraʿ, “scrupulous piety”.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا سَمِعَا نَصِيحَتِي وَوَعْظِي دَنَيَا مِنِّي فَأَقْتَنِصُهُمَا وَآكُلُهُمَا وَيَخْلُو لِي هَذَا الْمَكَانُ وَكُلَّمَا تَسَاقَطَ مِنْ ثَمَرِ النَّخْلَةِ يَكْفِينِي
sentences.tr: fa-idhā samiʿā naṣīḥatī wa-waʿẓī danayā minnī fa-aqtaniṣuhumā wa-ākuluhumā wa-yakhlū lī hādhā al-makānu wa-kullamā tasāqaṭa min thamari al-nakhlati yakfīnī
sentences.l: And when they-two-hear my-counsel and my-preaching, they-two-will-draw-near to-me, and I-shall-snatch-them-two and eat-them-two, and this place will-be-empty for-me, and whenever (any) of the fruit of the palm falls-down, it-suffices-me.”
sentences.i: Once they listen to my counsel and my preaching they will come close to me; then I shall snatch them and eat them, and this place will be mine alone, and whatever falls from the palm will keep me.”
sentences.n: danā min, “to come near to”. iqtanaṣa, “to catch, hunt down”. The ā of آكلهما is printed with madda. khalā li-, “to be left free for”. The print sets كلما as one word: kullamā, “whenever”, as pointed here; it could equally be kullu mā, “all that”, run together, with the same sense.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْوَرَشَانَ نَزَلَ هُوَ وَزَوْجَتُهُ مِنْ فَوْقِ النَّخْلَةِ بَعْدَ أَنْ نَثَرَا مَا عَلَيْهَا مِنَ الثَّمَرِ فَوَجَدَا الْقُنْفُذَ قَدْ نَقَلَ جَمِيعَ ذَلِكَ إِلَى جُحْرِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-warashāna nazala huwa wa-zawjatuhu min fawqi al-nakhlati baʿda an natharā mā ʿalayhā mina al-thamari fa-wajadā al-qunfudha qad naqala jamīʿa dhālika ilā juḥrihi
sentences.l: Then the ringdove came-down, he and his-wife, from the top of the palm after they-two-had-scattered what (was) upon-it of the fruit, and the-two found the hedgehog had carried all of that to his-hole.
sentences.i: Then the ringdove and his mate, having shaken down all the fruit that was on it, came down from the top of the palm, and found that the hedgehog had carried the whole of it off to his hole.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then (it happened that)”, the narrator's stock way of moving the story on. juḥr, “hole, burrow”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَرَشَانُ أَيُّهَا الْقُنْفُذُ الصَّالِحُ وَالْوَاعِظُ النَّاصِحُ إِنَّا لَمْ نَجِدْ لِلثَّمَرِ أَثَرًا وَلَا نَعْرِفُ لِقُوتِنَا غَيْرَهُ ثَمَرًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-warashānu ayyuhā al-qunfudhu al-ṣāliḥu wa-al-wāʿiẓu al-nāṣiḥu innā lam najid li-al-thamari atharan wa-lā naʿrifu li-qūtinā ghayrahu thamaran
sentences.l: And the ringdove said to-him: O the righteous hedgehog and the counselling preacher, indeed-we did-not find of-the fruit a trace, and we-do-not know for-our-food other-than-it (any) fruit.
sentences.i: The ringdove said to him, “O righteous hedgehog, O preacher who counsels well, we can find no trace of the fruit, and we know of no other fruit to live on.”
sentences.n: The address rhymes: al-ṣāliḥ / al-nāṣiḥ. li-al-thamari: li-, “of, belonging to”: “a trace of the fruit”. li-qūtinā: li-, “for”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَعَلَّهُ طَارَتْ بِهِ الرِّيَاحُ وَالْإِعْرَاضُ عَنِ الرِّزْقِ إِلَى الرَّازِقِ عَيْنُ الْفَلَاحِ فَالَّذِي شَقَّ الْأَشْدَاقَ لَا يَتْرُكُهَا بِلَا أَرْزَاقٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla laʿallahu ṭārat bihi al-riyāḥu wa-al-iʿrāḍu ʿani al-rizqi ilā al-rāziqi ʿaynu al-falāḥi fa-alladhī shaqqa al-ashdāqa lā yatrukuhā bi-lā arzāqin
sentences.l: And he-said: Perhaps-it — the winds flew with-it. And the turning-away from the provision to the Provider (is) the very-essence of the salvation; for He-who split the jaws does-not leave-them without provisions.
sentences.i: He said, “Perhaps the winds carried it off. And to turn away from one's daily bread to the One who provides it is the very heart of salvation: He who split open the jaws will not leave them without food.”
sentences.n: ṭāra bi-, “to fly off with”: bi- marks what is carried. The verb is feminine, agreeing with the broken plural riyāḥ. iʿrāḍ ʿan, “turning away from”. ʿayn, “eye”, also “the thing itself”: ʿayn al-falāḥ, “salvation itself”. al-Rāziq, “the Provider”, is God. ashdāq, plural of shidq, “corner of the mouth, jaw”. The sajʿ runs riyāḥ / falāḥ, then ashdāq / arzāq.

sentences.t: وَمَا زَالَ يَعِظُهُمَا بِتِلْكَ الْمَوَاعِظِ وَيُظْهِرُ لَهُمَا الْوَرَعَ بِزُخْرُفِ الْمَلَافِظِ حَتَّى رَكَنَا إِلَيْهِ وَأَقْبَلَا عَلَيْهِ وَدَخَلَا بَابَ وَكْرِهِ وَأَمِنَا مِنْ مَكْرِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā zāla yaʿiẓuhumā bi-tilka al-mawāʿiẓi wa-yuẓhiru lahumā al-waraʿa bi-zukhrufi al-malāfiẓi ḥattā rakanā ilayhi wa-aqbalā ʿalayhi wa-dakhalā bāba wakrihi wa-aminā min makrihi
sentences.l: And he-did-not cease preaching-to-them-two with those sermons, and showing to-them-two the scrupulousness with gilding of the utterances, until they-two leaned on-him and came-forward to-him, and entered the door of his-nest, and felt-safe from his-cunning.
sentences.i: And he kept preaching those sermons to them and showing them his piety in gilded words, until they trusted him and came to him, went in at the door of his den, and feared no trick from him.
sentences.n: mā zāla, “did not cease”, i.e. kept on. bi-tilka al-mawāʿiẓ: bi-, “with”, the means. zukhruf, “gilding, false ornament”; malāfiẓ, “utterances”, rhymes with mawāʿiẓ. aqbala ʿalā, “to turn toward, come to”. amina min, “to feel safe from”. The rhyme pairs run ilayhi / ʿalayhi and wakrihi / makrihi; the second pair is a jingle on wakr, “nest, den”, and makr, “cunning”.

sentences.t: فَوَثَبَ إِلَى الْبَابِ وَقَرَعَ الْأَنْيَابَ
sentences.tr: fa-wathaba ilā al-bābi wa-qaraʿa al-anyāba
sentences.l: And he-leapt to the door and gnashed the fangs.
sentences.i: Then he sprang to the door and ground his fangs.
sentences.n: qaraʿa, “to strike, knock”: here he clacks his teeth together like a beast about to bite. The rhyme bāb / anyāb.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى الْوَرَشَانُ مِنْهُ الْخَدِيعَةَ لَائِحَةً قَالَ لَهُ أَيْنَ اللَّيْلَةُ مِنَ الْبَارِحَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā al-warashānu minhu al-khadīʿata lāʾiḥatan qāla lahu ayna al-laylatu mina al-bāriḥati
sentences.l: And when the ringdove saw from-him the deceit showing-plain, he-said to-him: Where (is) the tonight from the last-night?
sentences.i: When the ringdove saw the deceit in him plain to see, he said to him, “How far tonight is from last night!
sentences.n: lāʾiḥa, “appearing, showing clearly”, a circumstantial accusative. ayna … min …, “where is … from …?”, asks how far apart two things are: al-bāriḥa is “last night”, and the saying means “how changed you are from what you were”.

sentences.t: أَمَا تَعْلَمُ أَنَّ لِلْمَظْلُومِينَ نَاصِرًا فَإِيَّاكَ وَالْمَكْرَ وَالْخَدِيعَةَ لِئَلَّا يُصِيبَكَ مَا أَصَابَ الْخَدَّاعِينَ الَّذِينَ مَكَرُوا بِالتَّاجِرِ
sentences.tr: a-mā taʿlamu anna li-al-maẓlūmīna nāṣiran fa-iyyāka wa-al-makra wa-al-khadīʿata li-allā yuṣībaka mā aṣāba al-khaddāʿīna alladhīna makarū bi-al-tājiri
sentences.l: Do-you-not know that for-the wronged-ones (there is) a helper? So beware-you and the cunning and the deceit, lest there-befall-you what befell the deceivers who plotted against-the merchant.
sentences.i: Do you not know that the wronged have a Helper? Beware of cunning and deceit, or what befell the swindlers who plotted against the merchant will befall you too.”
sentences.n: a-mā, “do … not?”, expecting yes. li-al-maẓlūmīna: li-, “belonging to”: “the wronged have a helper”. iyyāka wa-…, “beware of …”, the warning construction: the thing to avoid follows wa- in the accusative. li-allā, “lest”, printed لئلا. makara bi-, “to plot against”: the verb chooses bi-. The merchant's tale is only announced here.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْقُنْفُذُ وَكَيْفَ ذَلِكَ قَالَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-qunfudhu wa-kayfa dhālika qāla
sentences.l: And the hedgehog said: And how (was) that? He-said:
sentences.i: The hedgehog said, “And how was that?” He said:
sentences.n: The print has القنفل, a misprint for القنفذ, corrected here. The ringdove now begins the tale of the merchant and the swindlers.

sentences.t: بَلَغَنِي أَنَّ تَاجِرًا مِنْ مَدِينَةٍ يُقَالُ لَهَا سِنْدَه كَانَ ذَا مَالٍ وَاسِعٍ
sentences.tr: balaghanī anna tājiran min madīnatin yuqālu lahā Sindah kāna dhā mālin wāsiʿin
sentences.l: It-has-reached-me that a merchant from a city (which) is-said to-it Sindah was possessor of wide wealth.
sentences.i: “It has reached me that a merchant of a city called Sindah was a man of ample wealth.
sentences.n: The ringdove now tells the hedgehog the tale he promised, opening with balaghanī, “it has reached me”, Shahrazād's own formula. yuqālu lahā, “it is said to it”, that is, “which is called”. The town's name is printed سنده and is read here Sindah; the final ه is the print's, and the name is not otherwise known. dhū māl, “possessor of wealth”: dhā is its accusative as the predicate of kāna.

sentences.t: فَشَدَّ أَحْمَالًا وَجَهَّزَ مَتَاعًا وَخَرَجَ بِهِ إِلَى بَعْضِ الْمُدُنِ لِيَبِيعَهُ فِيهَا
sentences.tr: fa-shadda aḥmālan wa-jahhaza matāʿan wa-kharaja bihi ilā baʿḍi al-muduni li-yabīʿahu fīhā
sentences.l: And he-bound loads, and made-ready goods, and went-out with-it to some-of the cities, to-sell-it in-it.
sentences.i: He bound up loads and made ready his merchandise, and set out with it for one of the cities to sell it there.
sentences.n: shadda aḥmālan, “to tie up loads”, for the pack animals. matāʿ, “goods, wares”. kharaja bi-, “to go out with, take along”.

sentences.t: فَتَبِعَهُ رَجُلَانِ مِنَ الْمَكَرَةِ فَحَمَلَا مَا حَضَرَهُمَا مِنْ مَالٍ وَمَتَاعٍ وَأَظْهَرَا لِلتَّاجِرِ أَنَّهُمَا مِنَ التُّجَّارِ وَسَارَا مَعَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-tabiʿahu rajulāni mina al-makarati fa-ḥamalā mā ḥaḍarahumā min mālin wa-matāʿin wa-aẓharā li-al-tājiri annahumā mina al-tujjāri wa-sārā maʿahu
sentences.l: And two men of the cunning-ones followed-him, and they-loaded what was-at-hand-to-them of money and goods, and made-show to-the merchant that they-two (were) of the merchants, and they-travelled with-him.
sentences.i: Two sharpers followed him. They loaded up whatever money and goods they had to hand, made a show to the merchant of being merchants themselves, and travelled along with him.
sentences.n: makara, “cunning ones, tricksters”, plural of mākir. mā ḥaḍarahumā, “what was present to them”, whatever they could lay hands on. aẓhara, “to make appear, display”: they put on the look of merchants. The verbs are dual throughout: ḥamalā, aẓharā, sārā.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَزَلَا أَوَّلَ مَنْزِلٍ اتَّفَقَا عَلَى الْمَكْرِ بِهِ وَأَخْذِ مَامَعَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā nazalā awwala manzilin ittafaqā ʿalā al-makri bihi wa-akhdhi mā maʿahu
sentences.l: And when they-halted (at the) first halting-place, they-two-agreed upon the plotting against-him and the taking of what-(was)-with-him.
sentences.i: When they made the first halt, the two agreed to trick him and take everything he had.
sentences.n: nazala, “to dismount, halt”; manzil, “halting-place, stage”. makara bi-, “to plot against”: the verb takes bi-. akhdh, “taking”, is a verbal noun, genitive after ʿalā like al-makr. The print runs mā maʿahu, “what was with him”, together as one word, مامعه.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ كُلَّوَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمَا أَضْمَرَ الْمَكْرَ لِصَاحِبِهِ وَالْغَدْرَ بِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna kulla wāḥidin minhumā aḍmara al-makra li-ṣāḥibihi wa-al-ghadra bihi
sentences.l: Then indeed each-one of-them-two harboured the plotting for his-companion and the betraying of-him.
sentences.i: Then each of them secretly resolved to cheat his fellow and betray him.
sentences.n: aḍmara, “to conceal in the mind, harbour”. ghadara bi-, “to betray”: the verb takes bi-. kulla wāḥidin is accusative after inna; the print runs the two words together (كلواحد), and in the next sentence writes them apart.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ كُلُّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمَا فِي نَفْسِهِ لَوْ غَدَرْتُ بِصَاحِبِي لَصَفَى لِي الْوَقْتُ وَأَخَذْتُ جَمِيعَ هَذَا الْمَالِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla kullu wāḥidin minhumā fī nafsihi law ghadartu bi-ṣāḥibī la-ṣafā lī al-waqtu wa-akhadhtu jamīʿa hādhā al-māli
sentences.l: And each one of-them said in himself: If I-betrayed my-companion, then-would-be-clear for-me the time, and I-would-take all this wealth.
sentences.i: And each said to himself, “If I betray my companion, the times will be fair for me and I shall take all this wealth.”
sentences.n: law … la-, “if … then”, the unreal or hypothetical condition. ṣafā lī al-waqt, “the time became clear for me”: life would be untroubled. The print writes ṣafā with ى (صفى) for the usual صفا. The damma on غدرتُ is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَضْمَرَا لِبَعْضِهِمَا عَلَى نِيَّةٍ فَاسِدَةٍ
sentences.tr: thumma aḍmarā li-baʿḍihimā ʿalā niyyatin fāsidatin
sentences.l: Then they-two-harboured for each-other upon a corrupt intention.
sentences.i: So the two of them nursed a wicked intention against each other.
sentences.n: The phrasing is loose: aḍmara usually takes a direct object (“to harbour something”), and here it has only li-, “toward”, and ʿalā niyyatin fāsidatin, “upon a corrupt intent”. The sense is plain. li-baʿḍihimā, “for one another”, literally “for their some”.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذَ كُلٌّ مِنْهُمَا طَعَامًا وَجَعَلَ فِيهِ سُمًّا وَفَعَلَ الْآخَرُ مِثْلَهُ فِي طَعَامِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-akhadha kullun minhumā ṭaʿāman wa-jaʿala fīhi summan wa-faʿala al-ākharu mithlahu fī ṭaʿāmihi
sentences.l: And each of-them took food and put in-it poison, and the other did the-like-of-it in his-food.
sentences.i: Each of them took some food and put poison in it, and the other did the same with his.
sentences.n: The sentence starts with “each of them” and then adds “and the other did the same”, as though only one had been meant: the storyteller's grammar shifts mid-sentence, but both poison the food. summ, “poison”.

sentences.t: وَقَدَّمَ كُلُّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمَا طَعَامَهُ لِصَاحِبِهِ فَأَكَلَا مِنْ ذَلِكَ فَمَاتَا جَمِيعًا
sentences.tr: wa-qaddama kullu wāḥidin minhumā ṭaʿāmahu li-ṣāḥibihi fa-akalā min dhālika fa-mātā jamīʿan
sentences.l: And each one of-them set-before his-food to-his-companion; and they-two-ate of that, and they-two-died together.
sentences.i: Each set his food before his companion; they both ate of it, and both died.
sentences.n: qaddama li-, “to set before, serve to”: li- marks the one served. jamīʿan, “all together”.

sentences.t: وَكَانَا يَجْلِسَانِ مَعَ التَّاجِرِ وَيُحَدِّثَانِهِ فَلَمَّا غَابَا عَنْهُ وَأَبْطَأَا عَلَيْهِ فَتَّشَ عَلَيْهِمَا لِيَعْرِفَ خَبَرَهُمَا فَوَجَدَهُمَا مَيِّتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: wa-kānā yajlisāni maʿa al-tājiri wa-yuḥaddithānihi fa-lammā ghābā ʿanhu wa-abṭaʾā ʿalayhi fattasha ʿalayhimā li-yaʿrifa khabarahumā fa-wajadahumā mayyitayni
sentences.l: And they-two-used-to sit with the merchant and talk-with-him; and when they-were-absent from-him and were-slow upon-him, he-searched for-them to-know their-news, and he-found-them-two dead.
sentences.i: The two used to sit and talk with the merchant; so when they kept away and were long in coming, he went looking for them to learn what had become of them, and found them both dead.
sentences.n: kānā yajlisāni, “they used to sit”: kāna with an imperfect gives a habit. abṭaʾa ʿalā, “to be slow in coming to someone”; the hamza on its second alif (ابطأا) is the print's own. fattasha ʿalā, “to search for”, a colloquial turn (Classical fattasha takes a direct object). mayyitayni, “dead”, dual accusative.

sentences.t: فَعَلِمَ أَنَّهُمَا كَانَا مُحْتَالَيْنِ وَأَرَادَ الْمَكْرَبِهِ فَعَادَ مَكْرُهُمَا عَلَيْهِمَا وَسَلِمَ التَّاجِرُ وَأَخَذَ مَا كَانَ مَعَهُمَا
sentences.tr: fa-ʿalima annahumā kānā muḥtālayni wa-arāda al-makra bihi fa-ʿāda makruhumā ʿalayhimā wa-salima al-tājiru wa-akhadha mā kāna maʿahumā
sentences.l: And he-knew that they-two had-been tricksters and (each) wanted the plotting-against-him; and their-plot returned upon-them, and the merchant was-safe, and he-took what had-been with-them.
sentences.i: So he knew that they had been tricksters bent on cheating him. Their plot had come back upon themselves; the merchant was saved, and he took everything they had with them.”
sentences.n: muḥtāl, “trickster, one who uses ḥīla (stratagem)”. wa-arāda is singular where the two sharpers would call for the dual arādā; it is read here as “each of them wanted”, but the dual alif may simply have dropped out. Singular verbs with a dual subject are frequent in this text. The print runs al-makra bihi, “the plotting against him”, together as one word, المكربه. ʿāda ʿalā, “to come back upon”: the moral of the ringdove's tale, aimed at the hedgehog.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ لَقَدْ نَبَّهْتِنِي يَا شَهْرَ زَادُ عَلَي كُلِّ شَيْءٍ كُنْتُ غَافِلًا عَنْهُ فَتَزِيدِينِي مِنْ هَذِهِ الْأَمْثَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-maliku la-qad nabbahtinī yā Shahrazādu ʿalā kulli shayʾin kuntu ghāfilan ʿanhu fa-tazīdīnī min hādhihi al-amthāli
sentences.l: And the king said: Indeed you-have-made-me-aware, O Shahrazād, of every thing I-was heedless of-it; so-will-you-increase-me of these parables?
sentences.i: The king said, “You have opened my eyes, Shahrazād, to everything I had been blind to. Will you not give me more of these parables?”
sentences.n: nabbaha ʿalā, “to alert someone to”; -ti- is the feminine “you”. The print writes ʿalā with a dotted yāʾ (علي) and splits the name into شهر and زاد. ghāfil ʿan, “heedless of”. fa-tazīdīnī, “so you will add to me”, is a request in the form of a statement or question: “give me more”. mathal, plural amthāl, “likeness, parable, fable”. The damma on كنتُ is the print's own.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ أَنَّ رَجُلًا كَانَ عِنْدَهُ قِرْدٌ وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ الرَّجُلُ سَارِقًا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku anna rajulan kāna ʿindahu qirdun wa-kāna dhālika al-rajulu sāriqan
sentences.l: She said: It-has-reached-me, O king, that a man, there-was with-him an ape; and that man was a thief.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O king, that there was a man who had an ape, and this man was a thief.
sentences.n: A new tale begins, of the thief and his ape. ʿindahu, “with him”, is the usual way of saying “he had”. qird, “ape, monkey”.

sentences.t: لَا يَدْخُلُ إِلَى سُوقٍ مِنْ أَسْوَاقِ الْمَدِينَةِ الَّتِي هُوَ فِيهَا إِلَّا وَيَنْصَرِفُ مِنْهُ بِكَسْبٍ عَظِيمٍ
sentences.tr: lā yadkhulu ilā sūqin min aswāqi al-madīnati allatī huwa fīhā illā wa-yanṣarifu minhu bi-kasbin ʿaẓīmin
sentences.l: Not does-he-enter into a market of the markets of the city which he (is) in-it, except and-he-goes-away from-it with a great gain.
sentences.i: He never went into any market of the city he lived in without coming away from it with a great haul.
sentences.n: lā … illā wa-, “not … but that”: he never did the one without the other. sūq is usually feminine, but minhu treats it as masculine, as the lexicons allow and colloquial usage prefers. kasb, “gain, earnings”; bi- here is “with”.

sentences.t: فَاتَّفَقَ أَنَّهُ رَأَى يَوْمًا رَجُلًا يَحْمِلُ أَثْوَابًا مُقَطَّعَةً لِيَبِيعَهَا وَصَارَ يُنَادِي عَلَيْهَا فِى السُّوقِ فَلَا يَسُومُهَا أَحَدٌ
sentences.tr: fa-ittafaqa annahu raʾā yawman rajulan yaḥmilu athwāban muqaṭṭaʿatan li-yabīʿahā wa-ṣāra yunādī ʿalayhā fī al-sūqi fa-lā yasūmuhā aḥadun
sentences.l: And it-chanced that he saw one-day a man carrying garments cut-to-pieces to-sell-them, and he-began crying over-them in the market, and no-one would-bid-for-them.
sentences.i: One day it happened that he saw a man carrying some ragged clothes to sell. The man went crying them through the market, but no one would bid for them.
sentences.n: ittafaqa anna, “it chanced that”. muqaṭṭaʿa, “cut to pieces”: torn, tattered. ṣāra yunādī, “he began calling”; nādā ʿalā, “to cry (goods) for sale”. sāma, “to bid for, ask the price of”. فى is the print's spelling of fī.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ لَايَعْرِضُهَا عَلَى أَحَدٍ إِلَّا وَيَمْتَنِعُ مِنْ شِرَائُهَا
sentences.tr: wa-kāna lā yaʿriḍuhā ʿalā aḥadin illā wa-yamtaniʿu min shirāʾuhā
sentences.l: And he-would not offer-them to anyone except and-he-refuses from buying-them.
sentences.i: Whoever he offered them to refused to buy them.
sentences.n: ʿaraḍa ʿalā, “to show, offer to”. The print runs lā yaʿriḍuhā together (لايعرضها). After min the noun should be genitive, shirāʾihā (and the yāʾ-seat of the hamza suits a kasra); the print instead sets a damma on the hamza (شرائُها), and the word is read as printed, shirāʾuhā. The shadda in الّا is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَاتَّفَقَ أَنَّ السَّارِقَ الَّذِي مَعَهُ الْقِرْدُ رَأَى الشَّخْصَ الَّذِي مَعَهُ الثِّيَابُ الْمُقَطَّعَةُ وَكَانَ قَدْ وَضَعَهَا فِي بُقْجَةٍ وَجَلَسَ يَسْتَرِيحُ مِنَ التَّعَبِ
sentences.tr: fa-ittafaqa anna al-sāriqa alladhī maʿahu al-qirdu raʾā al-shakhṣa alladhī maʿahu al-thiyābu al-muqaṭṭaʿatu wa-kāna qad waḍaʿahā fī buqjatin wa-jalasa yastarīḥu mina al-taʿabi
sentences.l: And it-chanced that the thief who with-him (was) the ape saw the person who with-him (were) the clothes cut-to-pieces; and he-had put-them in a bundle and sat resting from the fatigue.
sentences.i: It so happened that the thief with the ape saw the man with the ragged clothes, who had put them in a bundle and sat down to rest from his weariness.
sentences.n: thiyāb is another plural of thawb, beside athwāb above. buqja, “a cloth bundle” (from Turkish bohça). kāna qad waḍaʿahā, “he had put them”, the pluperfect.

sentences.t: فَلَعِبَ الْقِرْدُ قُدَّامَهُ حَتَّى أَشْغَلَهُ بِالْفُرْجَةِ عَلَيْهِ وَاخْتَلَسَ مِنْهُ تِلْكَ الْبُقْجَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-laʿiba al-qirdu quddāmahu ḥattā ashghalahu bi-al-furjati ʿalayhi wa-ikhtalasa minhu tilka al-buqjata
sentences.l: And the ape played in-front-of-him until it-occupied-him with the gazing upon-it; and (the thief) snatched from-him that bundle.
sentences.i: The ape performed in front of him until he was wholly taken up with watching it, and the thief slipped the bundle away from him.
sentences.n: quddām, “in front of”. ashghala, “to occupy, distract”, for Classical shaghala. al-furja ʿalā, “looking on at, watching”, a colloquial word for an entertainment or show; bi- gives what kept him busy. ikhtalasa, “to steal by stealth, snatch”: its subject is the thief, not the ape, though the sentence does not say so.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَخَذَ الْقِرْدَ وَذَهَبَ إِلَى مَكَانٍ خَالٍ وَفَتَحَ الْبُقْجَةَ فَرَأَى تِلْكَ الثِّيَابَ الْمُقَطَّعَةَ
sentences.tr: thumma akhadha al-qirda wa-dhahaba ilā makānin khālin wa-fataḥa al-buqjata fa-raʾā tilka al-thiyāba al-muqaṭṭaʿata
sentences.l: Then he-took the ape and went to an empty place, and opened the bundle, and saw those clothes cut-to-pieces.
sentences.i: Then he took the ape and went off to a deserted spot, opened the bundle, and saw the ragged clothes.
sentences.n: The print has لى, a misprint for الى, corrected here: the alif-lām of ilā, “to”, has dropped out. khālin, “empty, deserted”, from khālī, loses its final -ī in the indefinite.

sentences.t: فَوَضَعَهَا فِي بُقْجَةٍ نَفِيسَةٍ وَذَهَبَ بِهَا إِلَى سُوقٍ آخَرَ وَعَرَضَ الْبُقْجَةَ لِلْبَيْعِ بِمَا فِيهَا وَاشْتَرَطَ أَنْ لَا تُفْتَحَ
sentences.tr: fa-waḍaʿahā fī buqjatin nafīsatin wa-dhahaba bihā ilā sūqin ākhara wa-ʿaraḍa al-buqjata li-al-bayʿi bi-mā fīhā wa-ishtaraṭa an lā tuftaḥa
sentences.l: And he-put-them in a precious bundle, and went with-it to another market, and offered the bundle for-the sale with what (was) in-it, and made-it-a-condition that it not be-opened.
sentences.i: He put them into a costly wrapper, took it to another market, and put the bundle up for sale with all it held, on condition that it was not to be opened.
sentences.n: dhahaba bi-, “to go with, take away”. bi-mā fīhā, “with what is in it”, contents and all. ishtaraṭa, “to stipulate, make a condition”. ākhar, “other”, is masculine, so sūq is again treated as masculine; it is diptote and takes -a.

sentences.t: وَرَغِبَ النَّاسُ فِيهَا لِقِلَّةِ الثَّمَنِ فَرَآهَا رَجُلٌ وَأَعْجَبَهُ نَفَاسَتُهَا فَاشْتَرَاهَا بِهَذَا الشَّرْطِ فَانْصَرَفَ بِهَا إِلَى مَنْزِلِهِ وَظَنَّ أَنَّهُ أَصَابَ
sentences.tr: wa-raghiba al-nāsu fīhā li-qillati al-thamani fa-raʾāhā rajulun wa-aʿjabahu nafāsatuhā fa-ishtarāhā bi-hādhā al-sharṭi fa-inṣarafa bihā ilā manzilihi wa-ẓanna annahu aṣāba
sentences.l: And the people desired it for-the smallness of the price; and a man saw-it, and its-preciousness pleased-him, and he-bought-it on this condition, and went-off with-it to his-house, and thought that he had-hit-the-mark.
sentences.i: People wanted it because the price was so low. A man saw it, was taken with how fine it looked, and bought it on that condition; he went off home with it, thinking he had done well.
sentences.n: raghiba fī, “to desire”: the verb takes fī. li- in li-qillati gives the reason, “because of”. aʿjabahu, “it pleased him”: the verb is masculine though its subject nafāsatuhā is feminine, allowed when the verb comes first. aṣāba, “to hit the mark”, to get it right.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْ زَوْجَتُهُ ذَلِكَ قَالَتْ مَا هَذَا قَالَ مَتَاعٌ نَفِيسٌ اشْتَرَيْتُهُ بِدُونِ الْقِيمَةِ لِأَ بِيعَهُ فَأٰخُذَ فَائِدَتَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾat zawjatuhu dhālika qālat mā hādhā qāla matāʿun nafīsun ishtaraytuhu bi-dūni al-qīmati li-abīʿahu fa-ākhudha fāʾidatahu
sentences.l: And when his-wife saw that, she-said: What (is) this? He-said: Precious goods; I-bought-it for-below the value, that-I-may-sell-it and-take its-profit.
sentences.i: When his wife saw it she said, “What is this?” He said, “Fine goods. I bought them for less than they are worth, to sell them and take the profit.”
sentences.n: bi-dūni al-qīma, “at below the value”: bi- gives the price. The print splits li-abīʿahu, “that I may sell it”, into لا and بيعه; the parts are kept apart here. fa-ākhudha, “and so take”, subjunctive, joined by fa- to li-abīʿahu. The print writes the word فأخذ, with a single hamzated alif for the ʾā of ākhudhu (Classical فآخذ); the dagger alif shows the long vowel. Unpointed, it could be mistaken for fa-akhadha, “and he took”, which the sense excludes.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ أَيُّهَا الْمَغْبُونُ أَ يُبَاعُ هَذَا الْمَتَاعُ بِأَقَلَّ مِنْ قِيمَتِهِ إِلَّا إِذَا كَانَ مَسْرُوقًا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu ayyuhā al-maghbūnu a-yubāʿu hādhā al-matāʿu bi-aqalla min qīmatihi illā idhā kāna masrūqan
sentences.l: And she-said to-him: O the cheated-one, is this merchandise sold for-less than its-value, except if it was stolen?
sentences.i: She said to him, “You dupe! Would anyone sell goods like these for less than they are worth, unless they were stolen?
sentences.n: maghbūn, “cheated, taken in (in a bargain)”, from ghabana. a-, the question particle, is printed as a separate word with its fatḥa (اَ). bi-aqalla, “for less”: bi- gives the price; aqall, diptote, takes -a after a preposition.

sentences.t: أَمَا تَعْلَمُ أَنَّ مَنِ اشْتَرَى شَيْأً وَلَمْ يُعَايِنْهُ كَانَ مُخْطِئًا وَكَانَ مَثَلُهُ كَمَثَلِ الْحَائِكِ
sentences.tr: a-mā taʿlamu anna mani ishtarā shayʾan wa-lam yuʿāyinhu kāna mukhṭiʾan wa-kāna mathaluhu ka-mathali al-ḥāʾiki
sentences.l: Do-you not know that whoever bought a-thing and did-not see-it-with-his-eyes was in-error, and his-likeness was like-the likeness of the weaver?
sentences.i: Do you not know that whoever buys a thing without looking it over is making a mistake, and is just like the weaver?”
sentences.n: ʿāyana, “to see with one's own eyes, inspect”. mukhṭiʾ, “one in error”. ka-mathali, “like the likeness of”: ka- and mathal say the same thing twice, the Qurʾānic idiom for a comparison. The print spells shayʾan شيأً, with hamza on alif and its own tanwīn. ḥāʾik, “weaver”: the wife now has a story of her own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا وَمَا قِصَّةُ الْحَائِكِ قَالَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā wa-mā qiṣṣatu al-ḥāʾiki qālat
sentences.l: And he-said to-her: And what (is) the story of the weaver? She-said:
sentences.i: He said to her, “And what is the story of the weaver?” She said:

sentences.t: بَلَغَنِي أَنَّ حَائِكًا كَانَ فِي بَعْضِ الْقُرَى وَكَانَ يَعْمَلُ فَلَا يَنَالُ الْقُوتَ إِلَّا بِجَهْدٍ
sentences.tr: balaghanī anna ḥāʾikan kāna fī baʿḍi al-qurā wa-kāna yaʿmalu fa-lā yanālu al-qūta illā bi-jahdin
sentences.l: It-has-reached-me that a weaver was in some (of) the villages, and he-was working, yet he-did-not obtain the daily-food except with toil.
sentences.i: “I have heard that there was once a weaver in a certain village who worked, yet could earn his daily bread only with great toil.
sentences.n: The wife, too, opens with balaghanī. qūt, “food, bare sustenance”. jahd, “toil, hardship”: bi- here means “with, by means of”.

sentences.t: فَاتَّفَقَ أَنَّ رَجُلًا مِنَ الْأَغْنِيَاءِ بِالْقُرْبِ مِنْ قَرْيَتِهِ صَنَعَ وَلِيمَةً فَدَعَا النَّاسَ إِلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ittafaqa anna rajulan mina al-aghniyāʾi bi-al-qurbi min qaryatihi ṣanaʿa walīmatan fa-daʿā al-nāsa ilayhā
sentences.l: And it-happened that a man of the rich, in-the-nearness of his-village, made a feast, and invited the people to-it.
sentences.i: It happened that a rich man who lived near his village gave a feast and invited people to it.
sentences.n: ittafaqa anna, “it chanced that”, the stock way of moving a story on. walīma, “a banquet, feast”. bi-al-qurb min, “near to”: bi- here means “in”, “in the nearness of”. The shaddas in فاتّفق and انّ are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَحَضَرَ الْحَائِكُ فَرَأَى النَّاسَ الَّذِينَ عَلَيْهِمُ الثِّيَابُ النَّاعِمَةُ يُقَدَّمُ لَهُمُ الْأَطْعِمَةُ الْفَاخِرَةُ وَصَاحِبُ الْمَنْزِلِ يُعَظِّمُهُمْ لِمَا رَأَى مِنْ حُسْنِ زِيِّهِمْ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥaḍara al-ḥāʾiku fa-raʾā al-nāsa alladhīna ʿalayhimu al-thiyābu al-nāʿimatu yuqaddamu lahumu al-aṭʿimatu al-fākhiratu wa-ṣāḥibu al-manzili yuʿaẓẓimuhum li-mā raʾā min ḥusni ziyyihim
sentences.l: And the weaver attended, and he-saw the people who (had) on-them the garments soft, (how) there-are-set-before them the foods splendid, and the master of the house honours-them for what he-saw of the beauty of their-dress.
sentences.i: The weaver came too, and he saw that the guests who wore fine soft clothes were served the choicest dishes, and that the master of the house treated them with honour because of their handsome dress.
sentences.n: yuqaddamu lahum, “is set before them”: a passive whose subject is al-aṭʿima, “the dishes”; the clause describes the guests without a linking word. zayy, “dress, attire”. li-mā raʾā, “because of what he saw”: li- gives the cause. The shadda in يعظّمهم is the print's own, and so is the hamza in رأى.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْحَائِكُ فِي نَفْسِهِ لَوْ بَدَّلْتُ هَذِهِ الصَّنْعَةَ بِصِنَاعَةٍ أَخَفَّ مُؤْنَةً مِنْهَا وَأَرْفَعَ رُتْبَةً وَأَكْثَرَ أُجْرَةً لَجَمَعْتُ مَالاً كَثِيرًا وَاشْتَرَيْتُ ثِيَابًا فَاخِرَةً لَارْتَفَعَ شَأْنِي وَعَظُمْتُ فِي أَعْيُنِ النَّاسِ وَصِرْتُ مِثْلَ هَؤُلَاءِ الْقَوْمِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ḥāʾiku fī nafsihi law baddaltu hādhihi al-ṣanʿata bi-ṣināʿatin akhaffa muʾnatan minhā wa-arfaʿa rutbatan wa-akthara ujratan la-jamaʿtu mālan kathīran wa-ishtaraytu thiyāban fākhiratan la-irtafaʿa shaʾnī wa-ʿaẓumtu fī aʿyuni al-nāsi wa-ṣirtu mithla hāʾulāʾi al-qawmi
sentences.l: And the weaver said in himself: If I-exchanged this craft for a trade lighter (in) burden than-it, and higher (in) rank, and more (in) wage, I-would-have-gathered wealth much, and bought garments splendid; my-standing would-have-risen, and I-would-have-grown-great in the eyes of the people, and become like these folk.
sentences.i: The weaver said to himself, ‘If I could exchange this craft for a trade less burdensome, higher in rank and better paid, I would gather a great deal of money and buy fine clothes; my standing would rise, I would be great in people's eyes, and I would become like these people.’
sentences.n: law … la-…, “if … then would …”: la- marks the answer to a law clause, and it is repeated on irtafaʿa. baddala X bi-Y, “to exchange X for Y”: bi- marks what one takes in exchange. ṣanʿa and ṣināʿa both mean “craft, trade”. muʾna, “burden, cost of upkeep”. The ḍamma in لجمعتُ and the tanwīn in مالاً are the print's own, as is the hamza in مؤنة, شأني and هؤلاء.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ نَظَرَ إِلَى بَعْضِ أَهْلِ الْمَلَاعِبِ الْحَاضِرِينَ فِى الْوَلِيمَةِ قَامَ وَصَعِدَ عَلَى سُورٍ عَالٍ مُرْتَفِعٍ شَاهِقٍ ثُمَّ رَمَى بِنَفْسِهِ مِنْهُ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ وَقَامَ قَائِمًا
sentences.tr: thumma innahu naẓara ilā baʿḍi ahli al-malāʿibi al-ḥāḍirīna fī al-walīmati qāma wa-ṣaʿida ʿalā sūrin ʿālin murtafiʿin shāhiqin thumma ramā bi-nafsihi minhu ilā al-arḍi wa-qāma qāʾiman
sentences.l: Then he looked at one of the people of the games, those present at the feast, (who) rose and climbed on a wall high, raised, towering; then he-threw himself from-it to the ground, and stood-up standing.
sentences.i: Then he watched one of the acrobats at the feast get up and climb a high wall, lofty and towering, throw himself from it to the ground, and come up on his feet.
sentences.n: ahl al-malāʿib, “the people of the games”: entertainers, tumblers. qāma wa-ṣaʿida follows with no linking word: it tells what the man he watched did. ramā bi-nafsihi, “threw himself”: with ramā, bi- marks what is thrown. qāma qāʾiman, “stood up standing”, stresses that he landed unhurt.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْحَائِكُ فِي نَفْسِهِ لَا بُدَّ أَنْ أَعْمَلَ مِثْلَ مَا عَمِلَ هَذَا وَلَا أَعْجَزُ مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ḥāʾiku fī nafsihi lā budda an aʿmala mithla mā ʿamila hādhā wa-lā aʿjazu minhu
sentences.l: And the weaver said in himself: There-is-no escape (but) that I-do the like of what this-one did; and (I am) not more-incapable than-he.
sentences.i: The weaver said to himself, ‘I must do just what this man has done; I am no less able than he is.’
sentences.n: lā budda an, “it is unavoidable that”: “I must”. wa-lā aʿjazu minhu is read here as the comparative of ʿājiz, “and I am no more incapable than he”. It could also be the verb, wa-lā aʿjizu, “and I shall not fall short”; but that verb normally takes ʿan, not min, so the comparative is preferred.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَ وَصَعِدَ عَلَى السُّورِ وَرَمَى نَفْسَهُ فَلَمَّا وَصَلَ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ انْدَقَّتْ عُنُقُهُ فَمَاتَ مِنْ سَاعَتِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma qāma wa-ṣaʿida ʿalā al-sūri wa-ramā nafsahu fa-lammā waṣala ilā al-arḍi indaqqat ʿunuquhu fa-māta min sāʿatihi
sentences.l: Then he-rose and climbed on the wall and threw himself; and when he-reached the ground, his-neck was-crushed, and he-died from his-hour.
sentences.i: Then he got up, climbed the wall and threw himself off; and when he reached the ground his neck broke, and he died on the spot.
sentences.n: Here ramā takes nafsahu directly, without the bi- of the acrobat's leap. indaqqa, “to be broken, crushed”; ʿunuq, “neck”, is feminine here, as the verb shows. min sāʿatihi, “from his hour”: at once.

sentences.t: وَإِنَّمَا أَخْبَرْتُكَ بِذَلِكَ لِتَجْعَلَ أَكْلَكَ مِنَ الْوَجْهِ الَّذِي تَعْلَمُ بِهِ وَتُحِيطُ بِهِ عِلْمًا وَلِئَلَّا يَدْخُلَكَ الشَّرَهُ فَتَرْغَبَ فِيمَا لَيْسَ مِنْ شَأْنِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-innamā akhbartuka bi-dhālika li-tajʿala aklaka mina al-wajhi alladhī taʿlamu bihi wa-tuḥīṭu bihi ʿilman wa-li-allā yadkhulaka al-sharahu fa-targhaba fīmā laysa min shaʾnika
sentences.l: And I-only told-you of that so-that you-make your-eating from the way which you-know (of) it and you-encompass it (in) knowledge, and so-that-not greed enters-you, and-you-desire what is-not of your-affair.
sentences.i: I have told you this only so that you will make your living by means you know and understand fully, and so that greed will not take hold of you and make you hanker after what is none of your business.”
sentences.n: The wife ends her story. akhbara bi-, “to tell of”: the verb chooses bi-. li-tajʿala, “so that you make”: li- of purpose, with the subjunctive. akl, “eating”: here one's livelihood. aḥāṭa bihi ʿilman, “to encompass a thing in knowledge”, to know it thoroughly; the verb chooses bi-. li-allā, “so that … not”. sharah, “greed”. The shadda in وانّما is the print's own, as are the hamzas in ولئلا and شأنك.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا زَوْجُهَا مَاكُلُّ عَالِمٍ يَسْلَمُ بِعِلْمِهِ وَلَاكُلُّ جَاهِلٍ يَعْطَبُ بِجَهْلِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā zawjuhā mā kullu ʿālimin yaslamu bi-ʿilmihi wa-lā kullu jāhilin yaʿṭabu bi-jahlihi
sentences.l: And her-husband said to-her: Not every knowing-one is-safe by his-knowledge, and not every ignorant-one perishes by his-ignorance.
sentences.i: Her husband answered her, “Not every man who knows is kept safe by his knowledge, and not every ignorant man is ruined by his ignorance.
sentences.n: A balanced pair: ʿālim / jāhil, yaslamu / yaʿṭabu, bi-ʿilmihi / bi-jahlihi; bi- gives the means, “by”. ʿaṭiba, “to perish, come to ruin”. ماكلّ and ولاكلّ are each set as one word in the print, mā kull and wa-lā kull run together; their shaddas are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ رَأَيْتُ الْحَاوِىَ الْخَبِيرَ بِالْحَيَّاتِ الْعَالِمَ بِهَا رَبَّمَا نَهَشَتْهُ الْحَيَّةُ فَتَقْتُلُهُ وَقَدْ يَظْفَرُ بِهَا الَّذِى لَا مَعْرِفَهَ لَهُ بِهَا وَلَا عِلْمَ عِنْدَةُ بِأَحْوَالِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-qad raʾaytu al-ḥāwiya al-khabīra bi-al-ḥayyāti al-ʿālima bihā rabbamā nahashathu al-ḥayyatu fa-taqtuluhu wa-qad yaẓfaru bihā alladhī lā maʿrifata lahu bihā wa-lā ʿilma ʿindahu bi-aḥwālihā
sentences.l: And I-have-seen the snake-charmer, the expert in the snakes, the knowing (of) them: often the snake bit-him and-kills-him; and sometimes gets-the-better of-it he-who (has) no knowledge to-him of-it, and no learning with-him of its-ways.
